paper_title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Agent evolution improves frozen LLM agents by refining persistent external artifacts such as prompts, skills, memories, and entire agent harnesses. It typically follows loop as shown in Figure 1b: proposer writes candidate artifacts, the resulting agent is evaluated on task set, and selection accepts the candidate artifacts that score higher. Evolution methods of this family have shown promise across benchmarks and models [24, 27, 37], making the prospect of systems that continuously improve their own workflows increasingly plausible. Yet the picture is far from settled. Studies often reach conflicting conclusions: the same methods flip between effective and ineffective across benchmarks, and their rankings trade places across papers. On TerminalBench [22] and other coding-agent benchmarks, evolution methods have repeatedly been reported to stall [7, 17, 29], while on other benchmarks each new method claims to outperform its predecessors [18, 24, 31, 43]. Whether evolution helps depends on the setting in ways the community cannot yet predict. This instability erodes confidence in this direction in both academia and industry, and rewards whichever method happened to be luckier at evaluation time. Yet unreliable evaluation affects more than the reported 1 Figure 1 (a) Four candidate moves on the same landscape, scored under high and low evaluation noise (thought bubble: score relative to the current artifact). Under high noise, worse candidate artifact scores highest. (b) Agent evolution as loop: proposer writes candidate artifacts, and selector accepts the artifacts with the highest noisy score. P1P3 are the predictions we test in Section 5. rankings of evolution methods. At the candidate level, the same kind of evaluation decides which artifacts to carry forward to the next round. As result, the evolution methods themselves become unreliable. We argue that this evaluation rests on an untested premise that its scores can identify the improvements evolution brings. We find that the premise fails at both levels where the scores are used. At the method level, the margins that separate methods in papers are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method: on Terminal-Bench, current common practice (Appendix D.3) can only identify the truly best of four text-artifact methods 33% of the time, barely above random guess (Section 4). At the candidate level, the selector picks the better of two candidate artifacts only about half the time, no better than coin flip (Section 5.2). Because each round accepts the artifact that happened to score highest, the scores go up but the artifacts do not get better (Section 5.3). Both failures trace to single constraint, which we state as hypothesis. The Resolution Hypothesis. The bottleneck of agent evolution is identifying which artifacts bring improvement, not proposing them. Why is identifying improvements so hard? Because model weights are frozen, an artifact helps only by changing the models behavior at inference time, while LLM trajectories also vary each time the agent attempts task. As result, separating true behavioral change from evaluation noise is difficult. We define the resolution of an evaluation pipeline as the smallest true improvement it can reliably distinguish from noise. Once the true improvement falls below this resolution, candidate selection degrades to chance, so little improvement accumulates during evolution (Figure 1a). Proposal determines how large the improvements on offer are; resolution determines how small an improvement can be and still be reliably identified. We test this hypothesis at much larger scale than current practice. Whereas prior work typically relies on single evolution run (Appendix D.3), we run each method 8 times per model and benchmark and evaluate each resulting artifact up to 16 times, totaling 1,030 independent evolution runs and over 2.1 million test trajectories. In total, the study covers seven agent evolution methods over six models and four agent benchmarks, plus nine further benchmarks on which we re-examine previously reported gains; to our knowledge, it is the largest reproducibility study of agent evolution to date. Our findings are: Method level (Section 4). Typical method margins are smaller than what single run can identify. The large historically reported gains are the clearest instance of our hypothesis: on those benchmarks, evolution succeeds by exploiting evaluation shortcuts that lift nearly every task at once, producing gains large enough to exceed the resolution of the evaluation, and stalls once the evaluation is repaired (Section 4.2). Candidate level (Section 5). We derive three predictions from the hypothesis. All three are supported by our experiments on Terminal-Bench: P1 Candidate pools contain artifacts that genuinely improve task performance: proposal is not the bottleneck (Section 5.1). P2 Common selection mechanismswhether based on execution scores or LLM judgmentsperform near chance at identifying the better of two candidate artifacts (Section 5.2). P3 Per-round selection errors compound across rounds, producing the large differences between independent runs of the same method that flip rankings (Section 5.3). Finally, we explore practical ways to address low evaluation resolution at both the candidate and method levels, from lower-variance behavioral checks to separate evaluations of proposers and selectors (Section 6). In conclusion, these findings suggest different perspective on agent evolution. The proposer determines what improvements are available, but evaluation resolution determines which improvements can be retained and accumulated. When this resolution is insufficient, true improvements are lost in noise, while large, easily detectable changes can dominate the evolution process even when they exploit evaluation shortcuts. Progress requires either enlarging the improvements being proposed or making smaller improvements reliably detectable. More broadly, developing higher-resolution feedback may be as important as developing more powerful evolution algorithms. All reproducible materials and trajectory data will be released upon the acceptance of this paper.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Agent evolution methods share common propose-evaluate-select loop but vary in what they evolve: prompts [2], skills [24, 37], memories [27, 43], or executable code [18, 42]. Several analyses document the fragility of this paradigm, e.g., sensitivity to run-to-run variance and task order [39], sparse feedbackdependent gains [19], and skill-induced failures or contamination from uncontrolled accumulation [7, 17, 29]. These findings point to noisy selection as shared failure mode, connecting to best-arm identification [12], uncertainty-aware RL evaluation [1], and the false-commit analysis of PACE [30]. Our work isolates the mechanism: we separate evaluation noise from run-to-run variance and use controlled pools to test proposal quality and selection reliability independently. Appendix gives full discussion.

sections.title: 3 Variance Decomposition and Experimental Setup
sections.content: To determine whether benchmark scores can identify improvements, we first need formal model that separates the stochasticity of the evolution algorithm from the noise of the evaluation instrument. This section defines the variance decomposition and outlines our experiments.

its expected score over repeated evaluations. A single observed score decomposes as ˆY (A) = Y (A) + ϵ, where

All seven methods on ALFWorld [32], SpreadsheetBench [20], OfficeQA [5], and Terminal-Bench v2.1 [22], each evolved and evaluated repeatedly to estimate τ and σ. Gain audit (Section 4.2). sections.title: 4 Resolution at the Method Level
sections.content: With both variance components measured, we can test whether standard evaluation practice can identify the method differences these papers report.

sections.title: 4.1 Single Reports Cannot Rank Methods
sections.content: For each method, model, and benchmark, we run evolution 8 times independently (16 times for the text-artifact methods on GPT-5.4 nano) and evaluate each resulting artifact 16 times on the held-out test split (8 times on Terminal-Bench and for harness methods). The unevolved baseline is evaluated equally often. We call method or the unevolved baseline on given model and benchmark configuration; in total, these experiments comprise 150 configurations, 1,030 independent evolution runs, and over 2.1 million test trajectories. We 4 estimate σ from how much repeated evaluations of the same artifact differ, and τ from how much the mean scores of the artifacts from different runs differ (Appendix B.2). Most method differences are below one single-run standard deviation. The standard deviation of the evaluation noise, σ, ranges from 1.0 to 3.7 percentage points (pp) on SpreadsheetBench, OfficeQA, and ALFWorld, and reaches 4.5 pp on Terminal-Bench, while run-to-run standard deviation τ ranges from 0 to 12.3 pp. Together, method evolved once and evaluated once has typical score standard deviation of 1.7 to 4.1 pp, the median over the configurations of each benchmark (values for every configuration: Table 6). Most method differences are smaller than this: for over 60% of pairs of configurations on the same model and benchmark, the gap between their all-run means falls below one standard deviation of single-run comparison (Figure 2a). The result holds method by method: for every method, 53% to 79% of its comparisons fall below one single-run standard deviation (Appendix D.1). Reported margins fall in the same range. sections.title: 4.2 Large Reported Gains Come from Evaluation Shortcuts
sections.content: Section 4.1 shows that typical method differences are too small for current evaluation to identify. Some benchmarks, however, show gains of 10 to 40 pp, far above the resolution of single run, both in the original papers and in our own runs, for example on SpreadsheetBench and LiveMathematicianBench (Appendix E.1). This suggests that evolution can find large improvements after all. The Resolution Hypothesis predicts exactly this pattern: evolution can accumulate an improvement only if the true improvement exceeds the resolution. An evaluation shortcut can produce such an improvement: single behavior that the evaluation rewards on most tasks of benchmark at once yields gain large enough for even noisy evaluation to identify. We test this prediction by auditing the largest reported gains on twelve benchmarks with three models, using two tests (design in Appendix E). One sentence reproduces the gain. Evolved artifacts contain many instructions, so large gain could come from many improvements or from single one. To find out, we audit, instruction by instruction, the artifacts released with GEPA and SkillOpt-Lite and those we evolved ourselves (an LLM agent flags candidate instructions, and we check each by hand), and append to the unevolved baseline only the one rule that appears most responsible for the gain. This single sentence nearly matches what full evolution achieved (Figure 3a): across the 27 modelbenchmark pairs with reported gain above 3 pp, it recovers median of 90% of the gain. The rule typically takes an evaluation shortcut: it adapts to grader that credits only one answer format, or to version of the benchmark, released with method, that departs from the official evaluation  (Table 9)  . We then repair each evaluation that admits shortcut, restoring the official evaluation or grading answers by meaning rather than surface form, and re-score the same artifacts. The median gain falls from 17.6 to 0.8 pp (Figure 3b), and on several benchmarks the repaired baseline leaves little headroom at all. Re-running the text-artifact methods under the repaired evaluations does not bring the gain back (Appendix E.3). This controlled contrast supports our argument: evolution succeeds when an artifact delivers an improvement large enough to exceed the resolution, and fails when only small, task-specific improvements remain. Two questions follow: do such small improvements exist at all, and if so, why does selection fail to accept them?

sections.title: 5 Resolution at the Candidate Level
sections.content: Progress within an evolution run depends on two conditions: proposals must offer true improvements, and selection must identify them. We examine both conditions on frozen candidate pools (Sections 5.1 and 5.2), then follow how selection errors behave across rounds (Section 5.3).

sections.title:
5.2 Selection Cannot Identify Them
Testing P2. Because candidate pools contain helpful skills (Section 5.1) yet evolution fails to accumulate them,
we next isolate the selection step. We construct the Selection Pool: n=100 skills generated from trajectories
on Terminal-Bench and DeepSWE, evaluated across 11 Terminal-Bench tasks spanning five difficulty levels
(Appendix F.1). Each selector observes only the first rollout (two rollouts for native SkillOpt-Lite and GEPA
selection), while true skill quality is measured on the remaining held-out rollouts (Appendix F.3). We test
whether standard selectors choose better skills more often than chance.
sections.content: Under realistic budgets, selection operates near chance. Greedy accept/reject on execution scores, if effective, would accept improvements and reject regressions with high reliability. Table 1 and the rank correlation 7 below show the opposite on all three metrics. In head-to-head comparisons, execution-based selection prefers the better artifact only 49.7% of the time, statistically indistinguishable from the 50% achieved by random selection. Regressions make up 30.5% of the pool but 62.1% of accepted candidates, so selection does not filter out regressions; the wide interval leaves open whether it is worse than random acceptance. The rank correlation between single execution score and posterior artifact quality is 0.054, essentially zero. The native parent-selection operators of SkillOpt-Lite and GEPA, which observe two rollouts per artifact rather than one, achieve 48.6% pairwise accuracy. Every execution-based selector in this study is statistically indistinguishable from random choice. No selector benefits from more candidates. Figure 4b plots the gain over baseline of the selected skill as the candidate budget grows from 1 to 100, averaged across the 11 tasks (per-task curves in Appendix F.4). While the Selection oracle (purple curve at the top) climbs steadily with as better skills enter the sample, every practical selector remains nearly flat around the random-selection baseline (gray dashed line). Even after examining all 100 candidates, no selector recovers the quality that an oracle already reaches within < 5 candidates. Model-based judges do not restore identification. Model-based judges are natural candidate for restoring identification, because they read the full trajectory rather than single terminal outcome [43, 45]. So one might hope they could tell helpful artifacts from harmful ones. Table 1 shows that this additional evidence does not help. No judge exhibits reliable pairwise accuracy. This may be because the judge has limited ability, while its reading noise is independent of evaluation noise. The two therefore accumulate rather than cancel out, introducing additional noise into the evaluation process. The consistency of this failure across such different selectors supports P2: under realistic budgets, standard selection mechanisms cannot identify helpful artifacts. Appendix F.3 examines whether repeated validation helps.

sections.title:
5.3 Noise Accumulates Across Rounds
Testing P3. Section 5.2 showed that individual selection steps discriminate at chance level. An evolution
run applies such a step in every round, so the relevant quantity is the cumulative effect of per-round
errors over rounds.
sections.content: In-loop gains reflect noise exploitation. Near-chance selection implies that most of the gain run records in its own validation scores, its in-loop gain, should disappear under careful re-evaluation. This is what the re-evaluation shows. We independently re-evaluate every artifact produced by eight evolution runs of SkillOpt-Lite and eight of GEPA on the same Terminal-Bench validation set, with eight rollouts per artifacttask pair where evolution used one (protocol in Appendix G). In-loop gains grow to 6.9 to 9.0 pp over the course of evolution, while re-evaluated gains remain between +0.4 and 3.2 pp (Figure 5). sections.title: 6 Towards Better Evaluation Resolution
sections.content: Because low evaluation resolution limits both candidate selection (Section 5) and method comparison (Section 4), we examine two practical ways to detect improvements that terminal pass/fail scores miss: finer-grained behavioral checks at the candidate level, and separate evaluations of proposers and selectors at the method level. Candidate level: finer-grained feedback. Terminal pass/fail rewards may obscure improvements in specific agent behaviors. promising direction is to supplement them with programmatic checks of intermediate behavior, such as unmasked failure diagnostics on verification commands or whether the agent runs test after editing file. Such checks do not fix selection by themselves, since an artifact that triggers more intermediate checks need not solve more tasks. They are however cheap diagnostics: in preliminary analysis (Appendix H), unmasked-diagnostic check rates exhibit 1357 lower evaluation noise than terminal pass/fail verdicts  (Table 13)  , and post-edit verification rates expose behavioral shifts that terminal verdicts miss. Method level: component-wise evaluation. Rather than comparing evolution methods only through noisy end-to-end scores, we encourage evaluating their components separately. For proposers, Quality@K curves measure the quality of the best candidate among proposals (Section 5.1). For selectors, selected-artifact quality curves measure the quality recovered from fixed candidate pool as the budget grows (Section 5.2). These diagnostics do not replace end-to-end evaluation, but they split one comparison that falls below the resolution into two that exceed it, revealing whether stagnation lies in proposal or in selection even when method-level margins are below the resolution of single run. At the reporting level, publishing both evaluation noise (ˆσ) and run-to-run variance (ˆτ ) alongside point scores lets readers judge directly whether claimed margin exceeds the evaluations resolution.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We propose hypothesis that agent evolution is bottlenecked not by proposing helpful artifacts but by identifying them. We provide evidence for this at both levels where evaluation scores are used: the margins separating published methods are comparable to the fluctuation of single run, so single-run rankings are largely determined by noise; helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection identifies them no better than chance, and these errors accumulate into run-to-run variance. The largest reported gains are consistent with this limit from the other sidethey exploit evaluation shortcuts and vanish once the evaluation is repaired. 9 less noisy As promising direction for future research, we suggest making evaluations resolution-aware: intermediate process metrics, component-wise diagnostics for proposers and selectors, and variance reporting that lets readers judge whether claimed margin exceeds the resolution.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Frozen weights only. We study agent evolution where model weights remain frozen and evolution operates only on external state (prompts, memories, skills, harnesses). Methods that update model weights via reinforcement learning operate under distinct gradient dynamics and may face different resolution constraints. Candidate pool scope. The candidate-level evidence is evaluated on Terminal-Bench v2.1 only: the Proposal Pool in Section 5.1 evaluates n=100 skills proposed from 10 Terminal-Bench training tasks across 10 disjoint test tasks, the Selection Pool in Section 5.2 evaluates n=100 skills proposed from Terminal-Bench and DeepSWE trajectories across 11 tasks, and the trajectory re-evaluation in Section 5.3 covers two methods and two models. Whether the conclusions hold for larger pools, different generation strategies, or other benchmark domains remains an open question. Model strength and resolution. Our grid includes models up to Kimi-K3, among the strongest available at the time of writing. We cannot rule out that future, substantially stronger models will exhibit lower evaluation noise and thereby better resolution. In our grid, evaluation noise shrinks for stronger models mainly where their success rate approaches the ceiling, as on ALFWorld (Appendix D.1), which is also where little headroom remains (Appendix E.4); on Terminal-Bench, where headroom is large, its median stays at 3.5 to 4.0 pp for all three models. Grid coverage. Seven methods, six models, and four agent benchmarks represent broad but not exhaustive survey. Methods that operate on fundamentally different artifact representations, or benchmarks with substantially different task structures, may exhibit different variance profiles. Beyond agent artifacts. Program evolution, which evolves the program that solves task and scores it deterministically, rather than the agents prompts, memories, skills, or harness code, has shown steadily accumulating gains in domains such as GPU kernel optimization [4], ARC-AGI-2 [23], and Atari policy search [14]. This paradigm structurally reduces evaluation noise through cheap parallel re-evaluation of deterministic code and more accessible program-environment diagnostics. Our analysis covers the current generation of text-artifact and harness evolution methods. Whether resolution similarly constrains program evolution is therefore an open question that our framework can address but our experiments do not.

sections.title: Use of AI Assistants
sections.content: We used AI coding assistants to write experiment and analysis code. All outputs were reviewed by the authors, who take full responsibility for them. In the gain audit, an LLM agent flags candidate instructions, each of which we check by hand (Section 4.2, Appendix E.1).

sections.title: A Extended Related Work
sections.content: Methods that evolve persistent artifacts. Recent efforts to improve frozen LLM agents without updating model weights organize along two dimensions: the macro-structure of the evolution loop, and the object being evolved. Along the structural dimension, methods include sequential refinement of single skill [37]; set-based evolution of prompt populations or agent archives [2, 42]; and memoryand playbook-based evolution [27, 40, 43]. Along the object dimension, methods evolve non-executable text artifacts, including skills distilled from trajectories [24], or executable code artifacts, including tools and harness components [18, 42]. Despite their structural variety, all such methods share the same loop: proposer produces candidate artifacts, an evaluator scores the resulting agent, and selector accepts higher-scoring candidates. Our analysis applies to this shared loop, and the constraint we identify holds across representations. Analyses of why evolving fails. parallel line of work documents the fragility of evolving agents and the unreliability of their benchmarks. Ye et al. [39] identify sensitivity to run variance and task order; Wang et al. [34] emphasize matched-budget baselines and held-out evaluation; and Liu et al. [19] find sparse, feedback-dependent gains across evolution rounds. SkillsBench measures the effects of curated skills across tasks [17], while subsequent analyses examine skill-induced failures [7] and contamination from uncontrolled skill accumulation [29]. SEAGym and continual-learning evaluations further distinguish intermediate gains from transfer, regression, and sustained improvement [33, 44]. Statistical reliability of selection. Noisy candidate selection relates to best-arm identification [12] and overfitting of model-selection criteria [3]. Uncertainty-aware evaluation is also established in deep reinforcement learning [1]. PACE directly studies false commits under repeated noisy comparisons and proposes an anytimevalid acceptance test [30]. Our study separates evaluation noise from variation across evolution runs and uses candidate pools to examine proposal quality and selection reliability separately.

sections.title: C Experimental Setup Shared Across Experiments
sections.content: This appendix describes the models, methods, and benchmarks that the experiment groups of Section 3.2 share. Table 5 lists which of them each group uses and the appendix that describes its protocol. C.1 Models and Inference Six models span the current capability spectrum: GPT-5.4 nano [25], GPT-5.6 Luna and Terra [26], DeepSeekV4-Flash-0731 [6], Kimi-K3 [13], and GLM-5.2 [9, 41]. Every role of method, whether solving tasks, reflecting on failures, or rewriting the artifact, uses the same model, so no method benefits from stronger model writing its artifacts. On ALFWorld, SpreadsheetBench, and OfficeQA, inference uses medium reasoning effort and at most 16,384 completion tokens per call. On Terminal-Bench, reasoning effort is left at each providers default. C.2 Methods and Evolution Budgets Seven methods span two artifact families. Text-artifact methods evolve prompts, skill documents, or memory banks: SkillOpt-Lite [31], lightweight variant of SkillOpt [37], GEPA [2], Trace2Skill [24], and ReasoningBank [27]. Harness methods evolve the agents own scaffolding: HarnessLens [36] edits its instructions, skills, and tool descriptions, and Meta-Harness [15] and AHE [18] edit its code. All methods run their official implementations, and each method has the same budget on every model. Table 2 summarizes what each method evolves, what its proposer writes, and how it decides what to accept; every validation score is one rollout per task. On Terminal-Bench, the splits have 18 training and 18 validation tasks. SkillOpt-Lite. On ALFWorld, SpreadsheetBench, and OfficeQA, SkillOpt-Lite follows the closed-loop example of its official release and runs at most 10 rounds. Each round proposes one edit from rollout of 40 training tasks and accepts it if one pass over the validation split beats the current skill by at least 2 points; an edit within 2 points is kept, but the reference score is not updated. The loop stops early after five consecutive rejected or unchanged rounds. On Terminal-Bench, it runs 3 rounds with batches of 12 training tasks and accepts an edit only if it raises the validation score. On ALFWorld, SpreadsheetBench, and OfficeQA, neither method has score-based selection; in the loop of Figure 1b, keeping every proposal is the degenerate selector that accepts every candidate, and like selector driven by noisy scores, it accepts regressions along with improvements. Meta-Harness returns the candidate with the highest training score; AHE scores each of its five versions once on the validation split and returns the best. Under the repaired grader the same rule is still worth about 6 pp, because some formulas use functions LibreOffice cannot evaluate, but on 39-task validation set this is two or three tasks, comparable to run-to-run noise. Only 2 of the 12 artifacts re-evolved under the repaired grader keep the behavior, although half of them state the rule in their text. Method nano DeepSeek Luna Benchmark OfficeQA SpreadsheetBench HotpotQA GEPA SkillOpt-Lite GEPA SkillOpt-Lite GEPA +8.6 SkillOpt-Lite 0.8 +3.1 SkillOpt-Lite +1.2 LiveMathematicianBench GEPA ALFWorld SpreadsheetBench OfficeQA HarnessLens +3.2 Meta-Harness 1.6 0.1 AHE +0.5 HarnessLens Meta-Harness +0.6 3.6 AHE HarnessLens 0.3 Meta-Harness +3.7 +2.8 AHE 0.6 +1.4 +0.9 +0.3 +1.9 +0.6 +0.0 +5.8 +8.9 +3.5 +0.0 +2.2 3.5 4.3 3.5 3.9 0.4 0.8 +30.3 +16.4 +31.7 +23.6 +1.6 0.3 +6.3 +0.1 +7.6 +8.8 1.1 0.3 +0.3 +2.8 +1.2 +3.7 Table 12 Gain (pp) of artifacts evolved under the repaired evaluation over the same-model baseline under that evaluation. Bold: 95% confidence interval excludes zero. LiveMathematicianBench is scored on questions without the leaked option. No shortcut was found in the ALFWorld evaluation, so its harness rows use the released evaluation. Harness methods. We also re-evolve HarnessLens, Meta-Harness, and AHE under the repaired evaluations on ALFWorld, SpreadsheetBench, and OfficeQA with GPT-5.4 nano, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and GPT-5.6 Luna, with 8 evolution runs and 8 evaluations each  (Table 12)  . On SpreadsheetBench and OfficeQA the gains are at most 9 pp, and HarnessLens returns its initial harness in 47 of 71 runs. Two larger gains need care. On ALFWorld, Meta-Harness and AHE improve DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GPT-5.6 Luna by 16 to 32 pp, because the initial agent keeps only the last two steps of its history; one run that changes nothing but this setting gains 29 pp. On SpreadsheetBench, AHE gains 11 to 13 pp for these two models on the 151 of 281 tasks whose instructions ask for formula, because the grader compares values and writing the computed value passes, but only 3 to 4 pp on the other tasks. Both gains come from single change that helps most tasks at once, the kind of gain that evolution can identify. E.4 Headroom After Repair Repairing an evaluation also shows how much room benchmark leaves for evolution. Terminal-Bench, which we did not audit, is included under its released evaluation. Benchmarks that no longer measure their target. On two benchmarks, the score can be earned without the capability the benchmark is meant to test. SearchQA: closed-book knowledge instead of retrieval. The benchmark is meant to test answering from retrieved search snippets, but the models answer as well without them. Under semantic grading, removing all snippets changes the score from 84.2 to 81.9 for GPT-5.4 nano, from 89.4 to 90.2 for DeepSeekV4-Flash, and from 89.8 to 90.7 for GPT-5.6 Luna. Snippets help only on the 126 of 1,400 questions whose snippets come from question-bank sites and contain both the clue and the answer. The remaining errors say little about the models: of 100 residual errors, which we attributed with an LLM and spot-checked by hand, 36 stem from wrong or ambiguous gold answers, such as Jeopardy clues that lost their category, or from answers that are in fact acceptable. The benchmark cannot even separate DeepSeek-V4-Flash from GPT-5.6 Luna (0.4 pp, 95% CI [1.5, 0.8]), and the released skill adds at most 1.6 pp. LiveMathematicianBench: one option is always correct. The benchmark turns theorems from recent arXiv papers into five-option questions that ask for the strongest statement that can be proved. Some questions include the option One of the remaining options is correct, but stronger result can be proven. Across the 177 questions of the released splits, this option appears in 85 and is the correct answer in all 85; it appears in 46 of the 106 test questions. For example, one test question is built from the theorem that every flow-admissible, cyclically 5-edge-connected, cubic signed graph has nowhere-zero 6-flow. The theorem itself is not among the options: one option weakens its conclusion to Z6-flow, two strengthen it to cyclic 4-edge-connectivity or 5-flow, one drops flow-admissibility, and the correct answer is the stronger-result option. model that always picks this option answers all 46 such test questions correctly without reading the mathematics, and the released skills entire gain comes from these questions. On the 60 test questions without the option, the baselines are 5061, yet no artifact improves on them; with 60 questions the confidence interval is about 5 pp. Little headroom. On several benchmarks the baseline, or the baseline plus one sentence, is already close to full marks once answers are graded correctly, so evolution has little left to gain. DocVQA. With semantic grading the baseline reaches 8894, and the released skill adds nothing. AIME 2025. DeepSeek-V4-Flash solves 96.5% of attempts without evolution. For all three models the repaired gains stay within 2.5 pp, comparable to the confidence interval of 30-problem test set. PUPA. The evolved artifacts reach 9697 for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GPT-5.6 Luna, and one sentence added to the baseline reaches the same level. ALFWorld, for strong models only. Gemini-3.7-flash, an additional model outside our main grid, starts at 96.3, and the best of our four text-artifact methods reaches 97.0. In the SkillOpt-Lite paper [31], both SkillOpt-Lite and its strongest competitor score 100.0 with GPT-5.4-mini, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5, so the benchmark can no longer rank methods for these models. Headroom without an identifiable gain. On other benchmarks much room is left, yet evolution gains little or nothing that the evaluation can identify. Terminal-Bench. It leaves the most room, 28 pp for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and 46 for GPT-5.6 Luna, yet the best method gains only 1.0 and 3.6 pp, below the standard deviation of single run (Section 4.1). OfficeQA. Under its official evaluation it leaves 3539 pp, but neither the released artifacts nor re-evolved text-artifact methods gain anything, and re-evolved harness methods gain at most 3.7 pp  (Table 12)  . LiveBench-Math. It leaves 1117 pp after repair, yet the repaired gains are only 0.2 to 1.3 pp. IFBench. Its gains of 2.73.8 pp are of the same order as its evaluation noise (Appendix E.2). Headroom with real gain. Three benchmarks keep gain that the repair does not remove, and in each case its source can be named. On HotpotQA, GEPA keeps 5.57.6 pp under semantic grading, and re-evolution traces the gain to retrieval: recall of supporting articles rises by about 10 pp. On SpreadsheetBench, 5.76.7 pp survive LibreOffice recalculation, but the re-evolved artifacts that keep gain do so by adapting to the recalculation engine, writing values and avoiding unsupported functions. On HoVer, gains of 813 pp come from retrieval strategies. These are the small, specific improvements whose identification Section 5 examines. E.5 Scope of the Audit The audit tests whether the largest reported gains need more than single rule; it does not show that an evolved artifact contains nothing else of value. Because we wrote each rule after inspecting the artifacts, the test shows that one rule is enough to reproduce gain, not that the gain requires this rule, and HoVer shows that the test fails when gain is spread over several strategies. The artifacts released with GEPA were evolved for GPT-4.1-mini, so their gains on our models are smaller than those in the original paper; we therefore compare, on the same model, the gain under the released evaluation with the one-rule result and with the repaired gain. Finally, repair can be incomplete. For re-evolution on LiveMathematicianBench, we balance 27 the leaked option: in as many questions as it is correct in, we replace wrong option with its text, so that it is correct only half the time where it appears. Half is still more often than the models answer these questions correctly (about 34% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash), so choosing the option remains profitable, and balancing only halves its benefit. We therefore score capability only on the questions that do not contain the option.

sections.title: F Candidate Pool and Selection
sections.content: F.1 Candidate Pools, Timeouts, and Evaluation Protocols Sections 5.1 and 5.2 evaluate two fixed pools of n=100 skills designed for the two stages of candidatelevel evaluation: the Proposal Pool, which tests out-of-sample skill transfer from 10 training tasks to 10 disjoint test tasks, and the Selection Pool, which benchmarks selectors and trajectory judges across 11 difficulty-stratified tasks. Proposal Pool (Section 5.1). To evaluate proposal quality without selection in the loop, an offline SkillOptLite-based proposer using DeepSeek-V4-Flash generates n=100 standalone skills from 78 execution trajectories across 10 Terminal-Bench v2.1 training tasks (kv-store-grpc, pypi-server, sqlite-db-truncate, path-tracing, filterjs-from-html, torch-tensor-parallelism, dna-insert, mcmc-sampling-stan, bn-fit-modify, tune-mjcf) following the protocol below. Each skill is then evaluated 16 times on each of 10 disjoint Terminal-Bench v2.1 test tasks (configure-git-webserver, break-filter-js-from-html, query-optimize, dna-assembly, rstan-to-pystan, vulnerablesecret, mailman, db-wal-recovery, torch-pipeline-parallelism, path-tracing-reverse), totaling 100 10 16 = 16,000 solver rollouts with binary whole-task rewards under native task verifiers. Original timeout vs. extended execution budgets. All 16,000 rollouts are executed with 2-hour (7,200 s) agent budget. Because Terminal-Bench tasks normally enforce shorter native timeouts (900 s, 1,200 s, or 1,800 per task), we also score five timeout cutoffs on the exact same set of finished trajectories by marking rollout as failed whenever agent elapsed time exceeds the cutoff: the tasks original timeout, 2, 3, 4, and the full 2h budget. Figure 9 shows Quality@K and its matched equal-quality null across all five cutoffs under our primary empirical-Bayes estimator (κmax=100; Appendix F.2): the pooled K=1 success rate rises from 39.69% under original timeouts through 45.15% (2), 48.14% (3), and 49.13% (4) to 49.23% at 2 h, while the K=100 excess above the matched null remains cleanly positive across every cutoff at +3.33, +3.22, +3.28, +3.30, and +3.41 pp (with non-overlapping 95% bands from 5 under original4 timeouts and from 4 at 2 h). Figure 10 displays all 10 individual test tasks under both original and 2 timeouts, showing that tasks whose multi-step compilation or rendering exceeds native limits (such as path-tracing-reverse, rising from 4.8% at original timeout to 41.4% at 2 h, and rstan-to-pystan, rising from 23.2% to 62.4%) explain most of the level shift between cutoffs, while near-homogeneous tasks track their matched equal-quality nulls closely within posterior bands. Selection Pool (Section 5.2). To benchmark selection operators and LLM trajectory judges across diverse candidates and task difficulty levels, Section 5.2 evaluates the Selection Pool: n=100 skills generated from execution trajectories across six Terminal-Bench v2.1 tasks and three DeepSWE tasks, rolled out on 11 Terminal-Bench tasks spanning five baseline difficulty levels (six source tasks and five held out from skill generation; listed in Appendix C). Every artifacttask pair receives 8 rollouts, extended to 15 for the ten highest-scoring artifacts per task, and the unevolved baseline receives 12 rollouts per task. Its per-task selection curves are reported in Appendix F.4. F.1.1 Proposer Research Protocol To generate n=100 distinct offline candidate skills from the training trajectories without an outer selection loop, the proposer launches parallel research sub-agents that inspect failure mechanisms on the training corpus and verify candidate fixes with small local probes. Below is the research and skill-authoring prompt used to synthesize the n=100 standalone skills in the Proposal Pool. 28 Figure 9 Effect of agent timeout cutoff on Quality@K vs. the matched equal-quality null on the Proposal Pool (10 disjoint Terminal-Bench v2.1 test tasks, n=100 skills, κmax=100 empirical-Bayes estimator). Panels (a)(e) evaluate the same 16,000 trajectories under progressively relaxed cutoffs: original per-task timeout (9001800 s), 2, 3, 4, and the full 2-hour budget. Panel (f) overlays the net excess above the matched null across all five cutoffs. Research & Skill Authoring Guidance Your goal is to investigate the training corpus in workspace/.skillopt/corpus/, uncover the concrete mechanisms behind task successes and failures, verify them, and translate them into one hundred complete, standalone actionable skills at workspace/artifacts/001/SKILL.md through workspace/artifacts/100/SKILL.md (each with its own report.md), backed by an auditable evidence report in workspace/report.md. There is no fixed reading quota, edit limit, or rigid output template. Read, search, write scripts, and run small executable probes in workspace/ as much as the evidence warrants. 1. Where to look: find the moment of wrong commitment Because task outcomes in the training pool are unbalanced, do not simply group failed runs by task name. Study both tasks with failures (comparing failed runs against passing runs on the same task to see the full workflow past early setup/install crashes) and pass-only or fail-only tasks (extracting how passing runs diagnose and recover from mid-run obstacles, or using local probes in workspace/ when no passing run exists). Focus on the critical decision points where an agent locks into flawed path: State and deliverable lifecycle: Check whether agents mutate raw inputs in-place before making safe backup, spend the entire budget in scratch experiments without maintaining valid working deliverable at the target path, or accidentally undo working state and stop required services during final cleanup. Unverified references & circular self-tests: Agents often believe flawed self-testor worse, modify correct implementation to match an inaccurate reference. Check whether the agent trusted library helper or reference script as an oracle without first verifying that its implicit behavior matches the task contract, or wrote checker that simply reused the generators own assumptions and offsets. Premature scaling without small probes: Check where agents launch expensive full-scale runs before using tiny run to verify interfaces, output structure, and how runtime, memory, or output sizes scale. Stopping at surface gains: In optimization or reconstruction tasks, check where agents stop after an initial improvement over naive baseline or rough approximation, versus how successful runs use concrete diagnostics (profiles, execution plans, structural parsers, or quantitative residuals) to locate and remove the remaining bottleneck. 2. Evidence discipline: verify mechanisms, do not just tell stories failed run and plausible narrative do not establish cause, and passing runs own explanation or code comment is only hypothesis. Inspect middle logs (beware output truncation): Long command outputs in your environment are truncated in the middle. Never assume broad dump showed the full trace. Before attributing failure to downstream visibility or configuration, inspect the middle of the transcript to verify whether upstream steps (such as compilation, linking, or installation) actually succeeded. 29 Figure 10 Per-task Quality@K (solid) and matched equal-quality null (dashed) across all 10 disjoint Terminal-Bench v2.1 test tasks of the Proposal Pool under the 2-hour budget (blue) and original per-task timeout (charcoal), using κmax=100 empirical Bayes; each panel uses its own vertical scale. Account for exact assertions: Repeated runs of task are not independent tasks, and failing the same test function does not mean failing for the same reason. Check the actual verifier output per run to distinguish early format or missing-file failures from downstream numerical or behavioral failures. Verify technical claims with small probes: Agents in passing runs sometimes rely on lucky approximations or state inaccurate formulas, byte layouts, or API rules. Before encoding specific mathematical formula, binary/database record format, parser behavior, or library rule into the skill, verify it with small executable probe in workspace/ or against local documentation. 3. Authoring skill.md: concrete actions, de-anchored from training literals High-level principles are research lenses for you (the proposer)they are not finished instructions for the solver. At the same time, skill that is over-fitted to one training problems surface details will fail to trigger on neighboring tasks. Strip training-instance literals, keep technical depth: Never leave training-specific filenames, JSON field names, sample IDs, or narrow one-task formulas as the trigger or example in skill.md. Broaden the trigger to the general technical scenario (e.g., corrupt database/file recovery rather than only truncated file; structured sequence/protocol assembly rather than one specific splicing formula), while keeping the concrete diagnostic commands, byte/format rules, and verification recipes sharp. Turn principles into decision-point checks: For each workflow you write, give the solver complete, executable playbook: 1. When it triggers and what to protect or establish first (e.g., full directory backup before first tool contact; tiny-budget schema and memory-growth check; saving an initial compilable baseline deliverable). 2. How to calibrate the reference check: Teach the solver to verify any third-party reference API on tiny 23 element hand-checked input before trusting it as an oracle, and to validate structured/composite outputs with an independent parser and end-to-end simulation (without reusing builder index offsets or dropping required protocol prefixes to guess grader behavior). 3. How to diagnose the next bottleneck: Provide concrete diagnostic loops (inspecting execution plans/profiles, reducing candidate sets before heavy computation, driving reconstruction via quantitative residuals, and checking multi-component service chains from fresh client). 4. Outputs and honest boundaries All training evidence is mounted read-only at workspace/.skillopt/corpus/ (see corpus/README.md for optional helpers). Use workspace/ for your own scripts, notes, and executable probes. Do not retrieve external benchmark solutions or test-set material. Save exactly one hundred complete standalone skills at the artifact paths above, each free of training task names, sample IDs, and task-local literal constants. Save concise, auditable report in workspace/report.md tracing the chain from what you read what you verified via probes what counterexamples or open gaps remain, citing exact message IDs, line ranges, and verifier what you wrote into the skill assertions. 30 F.2 Posterior Estimation of Quality@K Each artifacts per-task quality is latent success probability observed through handful of binary evaluations (Appendix F.1). Raw success counts are too noisy to rank individual artifacts reliably, so we regularize with an empirical-Bayes hierarchical model and define two complementary estimators. Hierarchical model. Let denote the pool size, si and ni the number of successes and total evaluations for artifact on given task, and θi [0, 1] its latent success probability. All artifacts share task-specific beta prior θi Beta(a, b), where the mean µ = a/(a+b) and concentration κ = a+b are estimated by cross-artifact method-of-moments from the pooled outcomes. In our primary estimator, κ is bounded in [0.25, κmax] with κmax=100 (already more than 6 the per-skill rollout budget m=16): whenever crossartifact sample variance does not exceed pure binomial sampling noise, ˆκ saturates at κmax rather than collapsing deterministically to zero-width point mass. For any finite κ, the posterior for each artifact is θi si, ni Beta(a+si, b+nisi), with posterior mean θi = (a+si)/(a+b+ni). We evaluate this same κmax=100 moment estimator identically on both observed pools and simulated equal-quality null pools, and test sensitivity across κmax {30, 100, 300, } below. Posterior Oracle. Quality@K asks: if we draw artifacts uniformly from the pool, how good is the best one? Let IK denote uniformly random size-K subset of the artifacts (baseline excluded). The posterior Oracle integrates this quantity over the full posterior: (cid:92)Quality@K Oracle = 100 Eθ (cid:20) EIK (cid:20) θi max IK (cid:21)(cid:21) . (7) We approximate the outer expectation with 8,000 posterior draws (256 draws per simulation inside each null dataset). Within each draw, the inner expectation is exact: sorting the sampled qualities in ascending order, the artifact at rank contributes with weight (cid:0) (cid:1) for K. Curves show draw means; shading denotes pointwise 95% credible intervals conditional on the fitted hyperparameters. (cid:1)/(cid:0) 1 1 Sensitivity to κmax. Figure 11 examines sensitivity of the 2-hour Quality@K curve on the Proposal Pool across κmax {30, 100, 300, }. An overly tight cap such as κmax = 30 forces substantial prior dispersion even when an equal-quality null exhibits no overdispersion, inflating the 2 matched null to 64.28% at K=100 so the +2.20 pp excess lies within overlapping bands. At κmax = 100, the 2 curve reaches 61.77% vs. 58.36% null (+3.41 pp, separating cleanly for 4), and relaxing κmax further to 300 or widens the excess smoothly to +4.75 pp (K 3) and +6.42 pp (K 2). Importantly, finite regularization at κmax = 100 avoids subtle point-mass degeneracy that arises under κmax = : on near-homogeneous tasks whose sample variance sits just below the binomial floor (e.g., dna-assembly or mailman), κmax = collapses the observed prior to δµ (a flat curve) whereas roughly half of pure-binomial null simulations happen to draw positive finite-sample overdispersion and finite ˆκ, nudging the simulated null mean slightly above the collapsed observed curve in per-task views. Bounding κmax = 100 keeps null-like tasks centered inside their matched null bands while every κmax 100 confirms the same positive headroom conclusion. Equal-quality null. Both estimators rise with even when all artifacts are equally good, because selecting the luckiest among more candidates yields higher expected score. To calibrate this statistical selection effect, we run 1,000 null simulations per task: all candidates are generated i.i.d. at the task-level pooled pass rate, and the exact same estimator (prior fitting and posterior Quality@K) is refit on each simulated pool. Each estimator has its own null curve (dashed in Figures 4a, 9, and 11). Null intervals describe central 95% simulation variability across equal-quality datasets rather than posterior uncertainty. Scope. Quality@K characterizes the finite pool of n=100 candidates, not the theoretical task optimum, and cross-task averages allow each task to select different skill. For the Selection Pool (Section 5.2), quality ground truth uses held-out rollout reference independent of each selectors observed rollouts (Appendix F.3). 31 Figure 11 Sensitivity of macro-averaged Quality@K vs. matched equal-quality null under the 2-hour budget to the upper concentration cap κmax {30, 100, 300, } of the empirical-Bayes Beta prior. tight cap (κmax=30) inflates dispersion in homogeneous null pools, whereas κmax=100 (primary) through unbounded (κmax=) behave consistently and cleanly separate observed from null. F.3 Selection Operators and Evaluation Metrics Independent-reference protocol. Each selector sees only the first rollout of each artifact (the native SkillOptLite and GEPA rows, the first two). Artifact quality is evaluated against held-out reference consisting of the remaining rollouts that the selector has not observed; the baseline reference likewise excludes its first two rollouts. This separation ensures that the quality ground truth used to assess selectors is independent of the information available to them. Artifact quality posteriors are fitted to this held-out evidence as described in Appendix F.2. All selectors share the same posterior draws, so selected quality is never larger than the oracle for the same draw, and all methods coincide at K=1. Native parent-selection ablation. The SkillOpt-Lite and GEPA rows (marked in Table 1) apply each methods own accept/reject logic to the first two rollout outcomes. SkillOpt-Lite replaces the current artifact only on strict improvement of the two-rollout mean; GEPA applies its frontier-pruning routine and samples parent in proportion to surviving frequency. These rows use the same held-out quality reference as the other selectors. Trajectory judges. DeepSeek-V4-Flash serves as the judge model on the 1,111 artifacttask pairs (including baselines) in the Terminal-Bench subset. Each call receives the task description, initial skill context, and the solver trajectory from the first rollout, without outcome labels. Pointwise scoring produces one score per pair (1,111 calls). Pairwise scoring evaluates 1,100 fixed pairs in both presentation orders (2,200 calls). The LLM judge (ACE) condition adapts the ACE Reflectors no-ground-truth template (error identification, root cause, corrective approach, and helpful/harmful/neutral tags), adding an explicit success-probability score. No ACE training loop or verifier feedback is used. Reported metrics. Pairwise accuracy: posterior probability that the selectors chosen artifact has higher latent quality, with ties broken uniformly. False acceptance: among accepted baseline replacements, the posterior fraction with quality below baseline. Improvement and regression rates: posterior probability that 32 the selected artifacts quality exceeds or falls below baseline. Spearman correlations are within-task; tasks with constant selector scores are excluded. Can Higher-Resolution Selection Improve Evolution? Our findings raise natural question: if we reduce evaluation noise during evolution by averaging many validation rollouts at every selection step, does evolution accumulate larger gains? To test this directly, we run SkillOpt-Lite for up to eight rounds across 16 independent evolution runs, averaging 16 validation rollouts per candidate instead of one (and evaluating final artifacts with 32 independent test rollouts per task). Averaging 16 validation rollouts raises the mean final test score across runs from 61.4% to 64.4%, and raises the best evolved artifacts test score from 64.8% to 72.7%. Inspecting the trajectories shows why: under single-rollout validation, an ordinary candidate occasionally draws an unusually high validation score by luck (e.g., 80%) and becomes the incumbent; subsequent candidates cannot beat this inflated threshold, stalling evolution within four rounds. Averaging 16 rollouts suppresses these false peaks so that accepted updates reflect real improvements, allowing the best evolved artifact to keep improving as more runs are launched. At the same time, 16 rollout validation is computationally expensive and makes greedy acceptance more conservative once strong incumbent is found, motivating the cheaper, finer-grained behavioral diagnostics explored in Section 6. F.4 Per-Task Selection Curves Figure 12 decomposes the aggregate selection curve of Figure 4b across each of the 11 Terminal-Bench v2.1 tasks in the Selection Pool (six source tasks T2, T5, T7, T9T11 and five held-out tasks T1, T3T4, T6, T8). Each panel plots selected-artifact success probability as function of the candidate budget under the held-out rollout reference (Appendix F.3). Equivalent budget. For each task and selector, the equivalent budget Keq is the smallest integer at which the oracles posterior mean quality reaches or exceeds the selectors quality at K=100. It measures how many candidates an oracle selector would need to match given selector after the latter has examined all n=100 candidates. 33 Figure 12 Per-task selection curves underlying Figure 4b across the 11 tasks of the Selection Pool. Each panel shows selected-artifact success probability under the held-out quality reference (Appendix F.3); the oracle and its credible band are clipped to the selector range. Trajectory Re-evaluation We recover eight independent evolution runs per method and model for SkillOpt-Lite and GEPA with DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GPT-5.6 Luna. The 119 distinct within-run artifact versions are independently re-evaluated on the same 18 Terminal-Bench validation tasks, targeting eight rollouts per artifacttask pair (versus one during evolution). Variance estimation. We estimate τ 2 as the sample variance of the eight task-averaged re-evaluation means, subtracting the mean estimated variance of their evaluation noise. For task success estimate ˆprjt from nrjt available repeats, the correction for run is 18 ˆprjt(1 ˆprjt)/(nrjt 1) on the probability scale. Unlike Appendix B.2, which reports ˆτ itself and therefore sets negative estimates to zero, we retain negative corrected estimates here, because we compare ˆτ 2 across rounds and clipping would bias the small early-round estimates upward. 2 (cid:80) Low-Variance Process Diagnostics Setup. We reuse the trajectories of the variance experiments (Section 4) on DeepSeek-V4-Flash. The terminal reward is the benchmarks pass/fail verdict. The process metric is the fraction of check commands along the trajectory whose failure diagnostics are not masked, where check command verifies intermediate state, such as running test after an edit, and its diagnostics are masked if the agent cannot tell from the output that something failed. Both quantities are computed per trajectory, so their variances are directly comparable. Estimation. For each configuration, we estimate the evaluation noise of each quantity with the within-artifact estimator of Appendix B.2, applied to the repeated evaluations of the same artifact. For the baseline and all seven methods, the evaluation noise of the process metric is 13 to 57 times smaller than that of the terminal reward. Behavioral shifts visible only to the process metric. The post-edit verification rate is the fraction of file modifications immediately followed by test execution or sanity check. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Trace2Skill raises this rate by +8.73 pp over baseline (z = 2.17 against the evaluation noise of the difference). On GPT-5.6 Luna, AHE lowers it by 17.98 pp (variance of the difference 0.0018, = 4.19). Neither shift is detectable in the terminal success rate of the same runs. Reading. process metric is diagnostic, not selector: candidate that passes more checks need not solve more tasks, and selector driven by such checks would face its own resolution question. Its value is that it makes behavioral change visible at resolutions where the terminal verdict is blind. 35 Method Baseline GEPA [2] HarnessLens [36] Meta-Harness [15] ReasoningBank [27] AHE [18] SkillOpt-Lite [31] Trace2Skill [24] reward σ2 σ2 0.073 0.074 0.056 0.084 0.075 0.095 0.071 0.077 behavior 0.0013 0.0026 0.0044 0.0015 0.0021 0.0022 0.0013 0.0021 Ratio 57 28 13 57 35 44 56 37 Table 13 Variance of the evaluation noise: terminal pass/fail vs. process metric (fraction of check commands without masked failure diagnostics), DeepSeek-V4-Flash.

sections.title: I Case Study
sections.content: I.1 Shareable Artifacts in the Candidate Pool Section 5.1 shows that candidate skills vary substantially even when single skill is shared across tasks. To illustrate what effective shared and task-specific skills look like in practice, this appendix prints three concrete skills from the Selection Pool (Appendix F.1): seed-027 and seed-099, tied for the best average gain across all 11 Terminal-Bench v2.1 tasks (+11.4 pp over baseline), and seed-058, which achieves perfect score on mteb-retrieve in every rollout yet adds little when shared globally. I.1.1 Artifact seed-027 (best average gain, +11.4 pp) Software Engineering Skill Read the task and relevant source before changing code. Preserve existing behavior while implementing the requested public API. Make coherent implementation across affected modules. Verify normal behavior and edge cases with focused tests. Treat every precise validation, parsing, error, export, and format rule in the prompt as an explicit assertion. Run relevant existing tests and address regressions. Agent pitfall: Substituting an idiomatic library name, conventional class name, or generalized reasonable signature for the exact exported symbol, function signature, return shape, or error-message string that the task explicitly names. Trigger: prompt that gives verbatim public identifier (class/function/entrypoint) or literal error/status text that hidden caller or assertion will match, while the agent invents library-flavored alternative such as generated servicer class name. Concrete correction: Before coding, extract every verbatim identifier, signature, empty/zero-value return rule, and error fragment from the task; export and reference those exact strings on the public surface and error paths, and add focused check asserting each named symbol and message exists exactly as spelled. Tiny verification: For spec that exports Mean(xs []int) (float64, error) and must return (0, nil) on an empty slice, expose exactly Mean (not computeMean) and return the documented (0, nil) instead of (-1, err), then confirm with one empty-input call. Agent pitfall: Improvising tokenization or embedding calls by hand (custom separators, toggling special-token flags, or single generic task/prompt name applied to both query and corpus) instead of delegating to the named model/package and its documented encoding conventions.
